newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin due back at Kremlin after surgery.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin due back at Kremlin after surgery.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin is due back to work on Monday after months of absence from the Kremlin because of ill health.
"In fact he is starting his second term as president with a delay of six months," Nikolai Svanidze, anchorman of the Zerkalo (Mirror) analytical programme on Russian Television, said on Saturday .

"We can sigh with relief now, Boris Nikolayevich is returning," said Anatoly Chubais, the Kremlin chief-of-staff, whose dismissal has been demanded by the communist opposition in parliament as a price for supporting the government's 1997 draft budget.
The draft is expected to be discussed by the State Duma lower house of parliament on the third and final reading at the end of the week.
Yeltsin, who suffered two heart attacks last year and had a quintuple heart bypass operation on November 5, had little time to run the affairs of state closely in 1996.

In February he launched a vigorous campaign for re-election. He then disappeared from public view shortly before winning a second term on July 3, and in September announced that he would undergo major heart surgery.
Since the operation, Yeltsin has made only brief public remarks and worked on a limited schedule.

Yeltsin's press secretary said on Saturday the president was expected to return on Sunday from the Rus residence 100 km (60 miles) from Moscow, where he has spent the last stage of his recovery, to his home in Gorky-9, a wooded area 20 km (12 miles) outside the capital.
But by Sunday evening there hadbeen no fresh report on where he was. "It has probably been decided to make no announcement on this," a Kremlin spokesman said.

On Friday, the 65-year-old leader gave his first television interview since the operation in which he said Russia needed an active president, new ideas and courage and promised an energetic return to work in the Kremlin.
"I feel the recovery period is over. I am returning to the Kremlin on Monday... I will be there at 9 a.m," Yeltsin said.
"The doctors have done their job and now it is up to the president," he said.
Yeltsin, who looked much thinner than before his surgery, spoke firmly and decisively though he appeared to move stiffly.
"There is no time for a warm-up. And besides, it is against my character. When I work, I work in earnest," he said.
The impulse to take quick, decisive action may be more than Yeltsin's doctors have recommended.
"The doctors recommend for a certain time a light regime -- a staged, gentle resumption of work in order not to overload the president," his spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Friday.

But in his interview Yeltsin promised swift and decisive action over the problems which had amassed during his absence - first of all unpaid wages and pensions, the peace process in the breakaway region of Chechnya and reform of the armed forces.
The president warned he will crack the whip on officials who have not worked hard enough in his absence, and said managers of business who do not pay taxes should lose their jobs.
Chubais said Yeltsin would meet his aides on Monday and talk by telephone to one of the leaders of the Group of Seven industrialised countries.
Interfax news agency quoted Chubais as saying there would be "no guests from outside" in the first two or three days of his stay in the Kremlin.
